value.overview: The Chipping Sparrow (Spizella passerina) is a small, slender New World sparrow of open woodlands, forest edges, scrub, parks, and other partly open habitats. Adults are especially recognizable by their bright rusty crown, gray face and breast, dark eyeline, and two white wing bars. It is widespread and common across much of North America. Most populations breed in temperate regions, while some southern populations remain year-round residents.
value.classification: The Chipping Sparrow belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows and towhees. Its scientific name is Spizella passerina.
value.identification: Adults have a rounded rusty-red crown, gray cheeks and underparts, a dark line through the eye, a pale bill with a dark tip, and two narrow white wing bars. The back is brown and streaked, while the rump is generally plain gray. In nonbreeding plumage the crown is duller and the facial pattern less striking. Juveniles are more heavily streaked overall and lack the strong adult head pattern. Its dry, rapid trill is distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Chipping Sparrow is distributed across much of Canada, the United States, Mexico, and parts of Central America. It favors open coniferous or mixed woodland, woodland edges, clearings, shrubby fields, orchards, riparian woodland, suburban areas, and parks. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or common migrant; it is recorded as an accidental or very rare visitor, with individual records mainly associated with open, landscaped, or disturbed habitats. It should therefore be considered an exceptional species in the country.
value.migrationStatus: Northern populations migrate south in autumn to the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America. Southern populations may be resident or undertake shorter movements. In Costa Rica, the Chipping Sparrow is an accidental or very rare species rather than a predictable seasonal migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly across Canada, the United States, and northern Mexico, usually in open woodland, woodland margins, shrubby clearings, and human-modified landscapes. The female generally builds a small cup nest of grasses, rootlets, and other plant fibers in a shrub or low tree, though nests may be placed higher. Clutches commonly contain three to five pale, spotted eggs. Both adults feed the young, which receive insects and other protein-rich foods before fledging.
value.dietFeeding: Seeds make up much of the adult diet, including seeds of grasses, weeds, and other small plants. During the breeding season, adults also take many insects and other arthropods, especially when feeding nestlings. Chipping Sparrows usually forage on the ground in open areas, scratching among leaf litter or picking seeds from bare soil and low vegetation. They may visit ground feeders and often feed in loose flocks outside the breeding season.
value.behavior: Chipping Sparrows are active, alert, and social outside the breeding season, often forming flocks with other sparrows and small ground-feeding birds. When disturbed, they may fly to a nearby elevated perch and give a sharp call. Males sing from exposed branches, shrubs, or utility wires during breeding. The species commonly uses open ground for feeding but retreats quickly into shrubs or trees when threatened. It is generally diurnal and frequently occurs near people where suitable habitat remains.

conservation.populationTrend: Recent range-wide monitoring indicates an overall decline in abundance, although trends vary among regions and populations.
conservation.threats: Potential pressures include the loss or maturation of open woodland and shrubby habitat, intensive agriculture, pesticide use, nest predation, and brood parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds in parts of the breeding range.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore open woodland, woodland edges, native shrubs, and weedy grassland mosaics. Reduce pesticide use, keep cats indoors, and provide native seed-producing plants. In Costa Rica, reporting unusual records through established bird-monitoring programs can help document this rare visitor and improve knowledge of its occurrence.
